title: Does a national curriculum help or hurt?

turns.speaker: Kem
turns.text: The review's out and it wants a slimmer core with much more school discretion around it.

turns.speaker: Padraig
turns.text: Which is what the last review said, and the one before that added everything back.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: It does cycle. Somebody notices the curriculum is overloaded, trims it, and then each subject lobbies its way back in.

turns.speaker: Kem
turns.text: What's the actual case for having one at all? Finland's is famously loose.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: Mobility, mostly. A child who moves school in March shouldn't arrive in a completely different syllabus.

turns.speaker: Padraig
turns.text: And it protects the subjects a struggling school would otherwise quietly drop. Music and languages go first, every time.

turns.speaker: Padraig
turns.text: Without a mandate, the schools under most pressure narrow fastest, and those serve the poorest intakes.

turns.speaker: Kem
turns.text: So flexibility is enjoyed mainly by schools that can afford it.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: That's the pattern, yes. Autonomy tends to reward the already comfortable.

turns.speaker: Kem
turns.text: The counter is that a prescribed curriculum plus high-stakes testing produces teaching to the test, which is its own narrowing.

turns.speaker: Padraig
turns.text: True, though that's the testing rather than the curriculum. You could keep one and change the other.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: Which nobody does, because the test is how anyone knows whether the curriculum happened.

turns.speaker: Kem
turns.text: So the accountability eats the content it was meant to protect.

points: A review recommends a slimmer core curriculum with greater school discretion, repeating a recurring cycle.
Liv notes curricula become overloaded as subjects lobby for inclusion after each trimming.
The case for a national curriculum rests on pupil mobility between schools.
Padraig argues it protects subjects like music and languages that pressured schools drop first, which disproportionately affects poorer intakes.
Autonomy therefore benefits schools that can already afford it.
Kem notes prescribed curricula with high-stakes testing cause teaching to the test, and they conclude accountability erodes the content it was meant to protect.
